title: What is a Spark Stage, how does the DAGScheduler determine stage boundaries (at every wide/shuffle dependency), and what is the relationship between stages, tasks, and partitions (one task per partition per stage)?
shortTitle: Spark Stage, the DAGScheduler, and stages/tasks/partitions
topicTitle: What is a Spark Stage, how does the DAGScheduler determine stage boundaries

s1_definition.profdef: A Spark Stage is a set of transformations that can run without any data shuffle, so all its tasks execute independently on their partitions and can be pipelined together. The DAGScheduler takes the logical DAG produced by an action and splits it into stages, cutting a new stage boundary at every wide dependency, because a shuffle requires all upstream tasks to finish before downstream tasks can start. Within a stage, Spark creates one task per partition, so the relationship is that a job contains stages, each stage contains tasks, and each task processes exactly one partition.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a multi-phase reporting project at the National Bank of India. A stage is one phase where every clerk can work entirely on their own box of files without passing anything to a neighbour. The DAGScheduler is the planner who draws the phase boundaries, and he draws a new boundary exactly wherever the files must be re-sorted and exchanged between teams — that re-sort is the shuffle. Inside any one phase, the work is split so that one clerk handles one box: one task per box of files. So the whole project is a sequence of phases, each phase is a pile of tasks, and each task is one box.
s1_definition.oneliner: A stage is a shuffle-free run of work, the DAGScheduler cuts stages at every wide dependency, and within each stage there is exactly one task per partition.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Spark Stage is a set of transformations that can run without any data shuffle, so all its tasks execute independently on their partitions and can be pipelined together. The DAGScheduler takes the logical DAG produced by an action and splits it into stages, cutting a new stage boundary at every wide dependency, because a shuffle requires all upstream tasks to finish before downstream tasks can start. Within a stage, Spark creates one task per partition, so the relationship is that a job contains stages, each stage contains tasks, and each task processes exactly one partition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a multi-phase reporting project at the National Bank of India. A stage is one phase where every clerk can work entirely on their own box of files without passing anything to a neighbour. The DAGScheduler is the planner who draws the phase boundaries, and he draws a new boundary exactly wherever the files must be re-sorted and exchanged between teams — that re-sort is the shuffle. Inside any one phase, the work is split so that one clerk handles one box: one task per box of files. So the whole project is a sequence of phases, each phase is a pile of tasks, and each task is one box.

**One line to remember:** A stage is a shuffle-free run of work, the DAGScheduler cuts stages at every wide dependency, and within each stage there is exactly one task per partition.

sections.s2_technical:
A stage is defined by the absence of a shuffle inside it. When transformations have only narrow dependencies — map, filter, flatMap — each partition's computation depends solely on one upstream partition, so there is no need to move data across the network, and Spark can pipeline the whole chain inside a single task. That pipelined, shuffle-free unit is a stage. The moment a wide dependency appears, data must be redistributed, and the work on the other side of that shuffle cannot begin until all the work before it has produced its shuffle output, so a stage boundary is required there.

The DAGScheduler is the component in the Driver that builds the stage graph. When an action triggers a job, the DAGScheduler walks the RDD or DataFrame lineage backwards from the action, and every time it encounters a wide dependency it marks a stage boundary. The result is a directed acyclic graph of stages, where shuffle-map stages produce shuffle output for the next stage and a final result stage produces the action's output. The scheduler submits stages in dependency order: a stage can only run once all the stages it depends on have completed, which is why a shuffle is a true synchronization barrier.

The relationship between stages, tasks, and partitions is precise and worth stating exactly. A job is the work triggered by one action. A job is divided into stages at shuffle boundaries. Each stage is divided into tasks, and the number of tasks in a stage equals the number of partitions of the data at that point, because Spark runs exactly one task per partition per stage. Each task runs the stage's pipelined computation on its single partition, independently of the other tasks, which is what makes the stage parallelizable across executor cores.

A senior nuance is that this structure is exactly what the Spark UI shows and is how you diagnose performance. The number of stages tells you how many shuffles the job has, the number of tasks per stage tells you the partition count and therefore the parallelism, and stragglers — a few tasks much slower than the rest — usually indicate data skew in a shuffle partition. Another nuance is that the number of post-shuffle partitions, and therefore the task count of the next stage, is controlled by configuration like the shuffle partitions setting, which you tune so that tasks are neither too few nor too small. In the bank, reading the stage and task view let me see instantly whether a slow nightly job was spending its time in a shuffle-heavy stage or waiting on a handful of skewed tasks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The reporting job must be cut into phases precisely where files are re-sorted. This is exactly the DAGScheduler drawing stage boundaries at wide dependencies.

Problem 2 — Within a phase, work must be split so the cluster runs it in parallel. This is exactly one task per partition per stage.

Problem 3 — The team must see how many phases and tasks a job has to diagnose it. This is exactly what inspecting stages and tasks provides.

The mini-project models this in Java. A `DagScheduler` takes a list of operations, each tagged narrow or wide, and groups consecutive narrow operations into a `Stage`, starting a new stage at each wide operation. It then creates one `Task` per partition for each stage and reports the stage graph. The demo builds a pipeline of filter, map (narrow), then groupBy (wide), then a final aggregate over Rajesh's and Priya's transactions, showing two stages and the task counts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data conceptually is transactions in four base partitions, and the post-shuffle partition count is set to three. The pipeline is filter, map, groupByKey, aggregate.

Step 1: The DAGScheduler starts stage zero with four partitions, because the base data has four partitions, so stage zero will have four tasks.

Step 2: The filter operation is narrow, so it is pipelined into stage zero. No boundary is drawn and nothing moves.

Step 3: The map operation is also narrow, so it too is pipelined into stage zero. Stage zero now contains filter and map and still has four tasks.

Step 4: The groupByKey operation is wide, so the scheduler draws a stage boundary. It closes stage zero and opens stage one with three partitions, the configured post-shuffle count, meaning stage one will have three tasks. The groupByKey belongs to this new reduce-side stage.

Step 5: The aggregate operation is narrow, so it is pipelined into stage one alongside the groupByKey. Stage one contains groupByKey and aggregate and has three tasks.

Step 6: The scheduler reports two stages — stage zero with four tasks running filter and map, and stage one with three tasks running groupByKey and aggregate — confirming that one shuffle produced two stages and that task counts equal partition counts.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] WIDE op 'groupByKey(accountId)' => stage boundary (shuffle). Starting new stage.
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Stage 0: ops=[filter(SAV2001|CUR3001), map(amount)], tasks=4 (one per partition)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Stage 1: ops=[groupByKey(accountId), aggregate(sum)], tasks=3 (one per partition)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Total stages = 2 (one shuffle => two stages)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Pipeline: filter → map → groupByKey(WIDE) → aggregate
    │
    ▼
  DAGScheduler walks lineage, cuts at WIDE deps
    │
  ┌───────────────────────── STAGE 0 (4 partitions → 4 tasks) ─────────────────────────┐
  │  filter  →  map     (both NARROW, pipelined in one task per partition)              │
  └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │ shuffle write (bucketed by accountId)
                       ══════════════ SHUFFLE BOUNDARY ══════════════
                                      │ shuffle read
  ┌───────────────────────── STAGE 1 (3 partitions → 3 tasks) ─────────────────────────┐
  │  groupByKey  →  aggregate   (reduce side, pipelined)                                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │
    ▼  result to Driver
  job = 2 stages ;  tasks per stage = partitions at that point
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Spark stage is a set of transformations that can run without any shuffle, so all its tasks operate independently on their own partitions and Spark can pipeline the whole chain inside one task. The reason a stage ends is a shuffle: the moment a wide dependency appears, data must be redistributed across the network, and the work on the other side cannot begin until every task before it has produced its shuffle output. That is exactly where a stage boundary must be, and it acts as a synchronization barrier.

The DAGScheduler is the component in the Driver that builds the stage graph. When an action triggers a job, it walks the lineage backwards from the action, and every time it hits a wide dependency it marks a stage boundary. The outcome is a directed acyclic graph of stages — shuffle-map stages that produce shuffle output and a final result stage — and the scheduler submits them in dependency order, so a stage runs only after the stages it depends on have completed. The relationship between stages, tasks, and partitions is precise: a job is the work from one action, a job is divided into stages at shuffle boundaries, each stage is divided into tasks, and there is exactly one task per partition per stage, which is what makes a stage parallelizable across executor cores.

In my project at the National Bank of India this structure was my primary diagnostic tool, because it is exactly what the Spark UI shows. The number of stages told me how many shuffles a job had, the task count per stage told me the partition count and therefore the parallelism, and a handful of straggler tasks running long after the rest almost always meant data skew in a shuffle partition. I also tuned the post-shuffle partition count so that the reduce-side stage had tasks that were neither too few, which underused the cluster, nor too many and tiny, which added scheduling overhead. Reading a slow nightly job in terms of stages, tasks, and partitions is how I turned a vague complaint into a precise fix.
